blocks.text: **Ethics** is the systematic study of what makes human action **right or wrong, good or bad** — the standards by which conduct is judged. Distinguish the neighbouring terms precisely: **morals** (personal/social codes actually held), **values** (enduring beliefs about what is worthwhile — honesty, courage), **laws** (state-enforced minimum conduct), **etiquette** (social manners). Ethics is broader than law: **everything legal is not ethical** (loopholes, unjust laws), and some ethical acts may even be illegal (civil disobedience). Branches: **meta-ethics** (what does 'good' mean?), **normative ethics** (what should I do? — consequentialism/**deontology**/virtue ethics), **applied ethics** (bioethics, environmental, administrative).

sections.heading: Consequences of ethics — and its absence

items: **For the individual**: integrity produces inner harmony, credibility and self-respect ('a clear conscience is a soft pillow'); unethical gain corrodes through guilt, fear and reputational fragility.

**For organisations**: ethical climate lowers transaction costs — trust replaces surveillance; unethical climates produce Enron/Satyam-style collapse (India's biggest corporate fraud, 2009 — a Hyderabad lesson).
**For administration**: ethics converts power into legitimacy; its absence produces corruption, capture, and citizen cynicism — the 'trust deficit' that makes every scheme costlier to run.
**For society & polity**: social capital, rule-of-law compliance, investment climate; ethical failure normalises shortcut culture — visible in tax evasion and everyday 'chalta hai'.
**For the environment & future generations**: intergenerational ethics (sustainability) — today's restraint is tomorrow's habitability.

items: **Thinkers to deploy**: Socrates ('the unexamined life is not worth living'), Aristotle (virtue as habit — 'we are what we repeatedly do'), Kant (categorical imperative — act only on universalisable maxims; persons as ends), Mill (greatest happiness), Gandhi (means-ends purity; **Seven Social Sins** — 'politics without principles, commerce without morality...'), Buddha (madhyama marga), Kautilya (praja-sukha as the ruler's dharma).

**Indian civilisational frame**: **dharma** as context-sensitive duty (svadharma), **Rta** (cosmic order), the Gita's **nishkama karma** — action with detachment from fruits — the classic answer to motivation-vs-consequence questions.

**AP/administrative colour**: use everyday service situations — certificate issuance, land mutation, welfare verification — where determinants (peer norms, political pressure, citizen desperation) collide; the essence-determinants-consequences triad maps exactly onto such cases.

blocks.text: Exam tip: This theme IS the definitional bedrock of the ethics section — memorise crisp one-line definitions (ethics/morals/values/law), the eight determinants, and five consequence domains. In case-study answers, explicitly name which determinant is operating; examiners reward that diagnostic vocabulary.

prelimsPointers: Ethics (Greek *ethos* = character/custom); moral philosophy's three branches: **meta-ethics, normative ethics, applied ethics**.
**Normative triad**: consequentialism (Bentham/Mill), deontology (Kant), virtue ethics (Aristotle).
**Kant's categorical imperative**: universalisability + humanity-as-end formulations.
**Gandhi's Seven Social Sins** (Young India, 1925) — wealth without work, politics without principles, etc.
**Milgram (1963)** obedience and **Zimbardo (1971)** Stanford prison experiments — situational determinants of conduct.
**Nishkama karma**: Bhagavad Gita II.47 — right to action, not to its fruits.
**Satyam scandal (2009)**: India's largest corporate accounting fraud — governance-ethics case from AP's own backyard.

The actual codes of right conduct held by a person or community — the lived counterpart of ethical theory.
Inquiry into the meaning and status of moral terms — whether 'good' is objective, subjective or emotive.
Kant's supreme moral law: act only on maxims you could will as universal law; treat humanity always as an end, never merely as a means.
The Gita's ideal of desireless action — performing one's duty without attachment to outcomes.

blocks.text: A second useful axis: ethics **at four levels** — individual (conscience), professional (codes), societal (norms) and global (human rights, climate justice). Case-study answers gain marks by identifying **which dimension and level** a dilemma sits in before resolving it.

sections.heading: Ethics in private and public relationships

blocks.text: **Private relationships** (family, friendship, love) run on **partiality**: loyalty, care, unconditional obligation — a parent rightly favours her child. **Public relationships** (officer–citizen, professional–client, leader–led) must run on **impartiality**: equal treatment, rule-boundness, public reason, accountability. The classic ethical failure of Indian public life is the **transfer of private ethics into public roles** — nepotism is family loyalty misapplied; the classic private failure is the reverse — treating intimates with bureaucratic coldness or transactional calculation.

items: **Continuities**: honesty, dignity, promise-keeping and non-cruelty bind both spheres — a person is one moral unit; **integrity means the spheres do not contradict** (the officer honest in office and in taxes at home).

**Differences**: (a) partiality vs impartiality; (b) discretion vs transparency (private life may keep secrets, public office must give reasons); (c) personal resources vs **trusteeship of public resources**; (d) consent-based vs power-asymmetric relations — hence stricter public standards.

**Conflict zones**: a friend seeks a favour in your official capacity (conflict of interest — disclose and recuse); family expectations vs posting integrity; whistle-blowing on a colleague-friend (public duty outweighs private loyalty — but with fair process); the **'godfather culture'** in transfers.

**Resolution tools**: publicity test (would it survive the front page?), reversibility test (roles reversed?), universalisability (Kant), and the **trusteeship** standard (Gandhi) — public power held for others.

items: **Exemplars**: Lal Bahadur Shastri (resigning as Railway Minister; refusing family use of official car), T.N. Seshan-era election discipline, **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's advice to services** on impartiality; contrast with dynastic capture and 'sifarish' culture.

**AP flavour**: a tahsildar processing her own relative's land mutation must recuse; a volunteer distributing pensions in his own street embodies the daily private-public interface AP's secretariat model creates — proximity aids delivery but multiplies conflict-of-interest situations: the design answer is disclosure norms + randomised verification + social audit.

Balanced close: the goal is not to sterilise private affection but to **fence it** — strong families build the values public life needs; strong institutions keep those loyalties from becoming favours.

prelimsPointers: Four dimensions of ethics: **descriptive, meta, normative, applied**.
Normative schools: **teleological** (consequences), **deontological** (duty), **virtue** (character), plus **care ethics** (Carol Gilligan).
**Conflict of interest** = clash between private interest and public duty; standard remedies: **disclosure, recusal, divestment**.
Gandhi's **trusteeship**: wealth and power held in trust for society.
**Lal Bahadur Shastri** resigned owning moral responsibility for the 1956 Ariyalur rail accident — the exemplar of public accountability.
Publicity test (Kantian/Rawlsian): an act is suspect if it cannot be publicly justified.
mainsAngles: Distinguish the dimensions of ethics and show where administrative ethics sits within applied ethics.
'Private virtue is no guarantee of public virtue, but private vice is a reliable warning' — discuss.
Partiality is the ethic of the family; impartiality the ethic of the state — examine the tensions when the two meet in a civil servant's life.
Nepotism is misplaced loyalty — analyse conflict-of-interest situations in administration and the safeguards against them.
In the era of doorstep delivery, proximity between officials and beneficiaries multiplies ethical friction — discuss with the AP secretariat-volunteer model.

glossary.definition: The branch of ethics resolving concrete domain-specific questions — administrative, medical, environmental, business, AI.
Deciding on relevant merits alone, without favour or bias toward relations, friends or groups — the first virtue of public office.
A situation where private interest could improperly influence official duty; managed by disclosure, recusal or divestment.
Gandhian doctrine that possessions and power are held in trust for society's benefit, not personal enjoyment.
Heuristic that conduct is ethical only if its justification could be openly stated without shame — a screen for hidden partiality.
Normative approach (Gilligan, Noddings) centring relationships, empathy and responsiveness — a corrective to purely rule-based ethics.

blocks.text: **Integrity** (Latin *integer* — whole) is the **consistency of values, words and actions across situations and audiences** — being the same person in the file, in the field and at home. It is broader than honesty: honesty is truth-telling; integrity is **wholeness** — incorruptibility, moral courage, and refusal to compartmentalise. Types worth naming: **financial integrity** (no illicit gain), **intellectual integrity** (following evidence against convenience), **moral integrity** (acting on professed values), and **institutional integrity** (an organisation's fidelity to its purpose — Lokpal, ECI debates).

sections.heading: The architecture of accountability in Indian public service

items: **Internal**: conduct rules, hierarchy, APAR/360°, vigilance officers, departmental inquiries (Art 311 procedure) — fast in theory, protective in practice.
**Legislative**: questions, committees (PAC/Estimates/DRSC), CAG audit — the classic chain; weakened by shrinking House time.
**Judicial**: review of administrative action, PC Act prosecutions, continuing mandamus.
**Independent bodies**: CVC (superintendence), Lokpal (2013 Act; functional since 2019) & **Lokayuktas**, CIC, NHRC — the ombudsman layer.
**Social**: RTI, social audit (AP's SSAAT), citizen charters with penalties, media & civil society — accountability's newest, most democratic ring.

**Diagnosis (2nd ARC, 4th Report)**: India punishes honest error and misses calibrated dishonesty — recommendations: protect bona fide action (**now PC Act Sec 17A**), swift traps for the corrupt, simplified disciplinary process, and **ethical competence in recruitment and training** (now Mission Karmayogi's behavioural frame).

items: **Reduce opportunity**: process re-engineering, e-delivery (fewer discretionary touchpoints — AP's Mee-Seva/DBT lineage), transparent postings, e-procurement (GeM).
**Raise the cost**: certain and swift (not merely severe) sanction; asset-disproportion cases; **forfeiture laws**; protect whistle-blowers (2014 Act's non-operation is the standing gap).

**Grow the conscience**: ethics training with dilemmas not sermons (Karmayogi), oath-and-onboarding rituals, integrity role-modelling by seniors — 'the tone at the top sets the ethics budget of the middle'.

**Exemplars to cite**: **E. Sreedharan** (Delhi Metro — schedule and probity as culture), **T.N. Seshan** (institutional assertion), **S.R. Sankaran** (the 'people's IAS officer' of undivided AP — austere, tribal-welfare pioneer, refused awards) — Sankaran is the perfect APPSC exemplar.
Balanced close: integrity is personal, but **probity is infrastructural** — built from systems that make honesty easy and dishonesty costly.

blocks.text: Exam tip: Define integrity vs honesty vs probity in the first three lines — that distinction alone separates answers. Then one accountability map (five rings), one 2nd ARC recommendation, one AP exemplar (S.R. Sankaran). For case studies, integrity = consistency under pressure; show the pressure, then the consistency.

prelimsPointers: **2nd ARC 4th Report: 'Ethics in Governance'** — the master document for this theme.
**PC Act 1988, amended 2018**: taking a bribe redefined (Sec 7), **giving** a bribe an offence (Sec 8), **Sec 17A** prior-approval shield for official decisions, time-bound trials.
**Lokpal**: 2013 Act; chairperson + up to 8 members (50% judicial; 50% from SC/ST/OBC/minorities/women); first Lokpal appointed **2019**.
**CVC**: statutory (2003); Integrity Pact and integrity-index initiatives in procurement.
**Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014** — assented but rules un-notified; 2015 dilution Bill pending.
**S.R. Sankaran (IAS, undivided AP)** — exemplar of austere, welfare-first service; key figure behind bonded-labour abolition follow-up and SC/ST sub-plan thinking.
Conduct Rules: **CCS (Conduct) Rules 1964 / AIS (Conduct) Rules 1968**.
mainsAngles: Integrity is wholeness, honesty is only truthfulness — elaborate the distinction and its significance for public service.
India's accountability regime deters the honest more than the corrupt — critically examine with the 2nd ARC and Section 17A.
Map the five rings of accountability around an Indian civil servant and evaluate their relative effectiveness.
Institutional integrity matters as much as personal integrity — discuss with reference to the Election Commission and Lokpal debates.

glossary.definition: Consistency of values, words and deeds across contexts — incorruptible wholeness of character; broader than honesty.
Demonstrated adherence to the highest standards of rectitude in public office — integrity as verified public practice.
The duty of power-holders to explain their use of public authority and to bear consequences for its misuse.
CVC-promoted agreement between procurer and bidders forswearing bribery, monitored by independent external monitors.
2018 provision requiring prior approval before inquiry into decisions taken by public servants in official functions — the honest-error shield.
An institution's fidelity to its constitutional purpose, protected through appointment quality, autonomy and transparency (phrase from the SC's CVC appointment ruling, 2011).
